main_point.en: Jesus doesn’t turn us away when we go to Him in faith.

christ_connection.en: Jesus responded to those who came to Him in faith for physical healing. In a greater way, Jesus forgives and restores all who come to Him in faith for salvation from sin.

title.en: We Can Take Our Desperation to Jesus

content.en: 40 Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. 41 And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus’ feet, he implored him to come to his house, 42 for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him. 43 And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. 44 She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased. 45 And Jesus said, “Who was it that touched me?” When all denied it, Peter said, “Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!”

46 But Jesus said, “Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.” 47 And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. 48 And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.” 49 While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler’s house came and said, “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” 50 But Jesus on hearing this answered him, “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.” 51 And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. 52 And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, “Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.” 53 And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. 54 But taking her by the hand he called, saying, “Child, arise.” 55 And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. 56 And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

Leaders: The Lord doesn’t push us away when we run to Him in desperation—with our sin, with our shame, with our struggles. More than ever, students need to hear this truth. Show them how to run to Jesus.

title.en: We Can Take Our Desperation to Jesus

content.en: “The malady itself must have been distressing and it had social consequences as well as physical. Because this complaint made her ceremonially unclean (Lev. 15:25), the sufferer was not permitted to take any part in temple worship or the like. Her uncleanness was readily communicable to other people (a touch was all that was needed, Lev. 15:27). She would accordingly have been avoided lest others contract from her an uncleanness which, though temporary, was troublesome.”"

“Jesus returned, apparently across the sea to Capernaum, to the crowds He normally faced see vv. 4,19). These crowds were eager to see Him, view His miracles, and find healing for their sick family and friends. Ironically, the first to meet Him as He returned from pig and demon country was a synagogue ruler. He was responsible for arranging the synagogue for meetings and probably leading the council of elders in the synagogue. Jairus had no time to see if all was kosher. Jesus’s state of purity was not a priority with him. Only one thing mattered: his dying daughter. Falling at Jesus’s feet in humility, respect, and reverence, Jairus was transformed from a respected leader to a desperate beggar.”

Healed yow’ is literally saved you. It was not simply the woman’s touching of Jesus’s garment that healed her, for others pressed against Jesus as well; it was the faith that caused her to touch Jesus that brought healing. Yet something more happened than the cessation of her bleeding. She experienced physical healing but even more. If Jesus’s concern for her involved physical healing only, what occurred in Luke 8:45-48 could have been omitted. Luke reported that Jesus sought out the woman because something greater than physical healing was taking place. Through faith the woman also received spiritual healing.”¹³

In today’s passage, we find a common thread of faith woven through the stories of two very different people: one, a religious leader named Jairus; the other, an unnamed woman, ostracized and “unclean.” Jairus was a leader in the synagogue, likely known by Jews in the area. Jairus falling at Jesus’s feet and pleading for Him to heal his daughter was a significant declaration of belief in Jesus’s power. Jairus exhibited brave faith in a time when groups like the Pharisees so openly opposed and threatened Jesus. His desperation was a catalyst for faith and healing. Likewise, the woman was desperate for healing; her problem with bleeding was more than just a medical issue. According to the law, the bleeding she experienced made her ceremonially unclean, unable to participate in worship with her people. Anyone who touched her would’ve been unclean as well. The woman had been separated from society and unable to worship at the temple for twelve years with no hope in sight. By law, her touching Jesus’s robe would’ve rendered Him unclean as well; instead, Jesus cleansed and restored her because of her faith! Leaders: Approach your discussion about the woman suffering from bleeding with sensitivity and maturity. Some students may find the medical nature of the story uncomfortable; root the discussion in her prolonged physical suffering and the social isolation she endured.

Biblical faith is the resting, or trusting, in Jesus alone for salvation (John 3:16-21). More than being simply a mental agreement of historical facts, genuine faith begins with a recognition and confession of the truth of the gospel (1 John 4:13-16), followed by a receiving of Jesus as Lord and Savior of one’s life (John 1:10-13). Biblical faith is not blind faith, for it rests on the historical life, death, and resurrection of Jesus.
LORD, THANK YOU FOR YOUR GREAT LOVE FOR US. THANK YOU FOR THE REMINDER THAT WE CAN COME TO YOU WITH OUR DESPERATION. YOU HEAL US FROM OUR SIN, AND WE LIVE IN GRATEFUL WORSHIP.
Not only did Luke write a Gospel account, but he was also a doctor. Because he understood on a deeper level the illnesses and ailments healed by Jesus, he also understood the power of Jesus!¹⁴

instructions.en:
These optional activities are designed to help your students interact. You'll find a Discussion Activity and a Cultural Connection, which touches on a relevant topic in today’s teen culture. Each group is different, so adapt these activities to fit your group’s needs. The goal is for students to connect more to the lesson as they connect to the topic and to one another.

Ask the following questions, allowing time for students to share responses:

question.en: HOW DOES IT FEEL WHEN YOU HAVE TO RELY ON SOMEONE ELSE TO DO SOMETHING THAT’S IMPORTANT TO YOU? ARE THERE PEOPLE YOU’D TRUST MORE THAN OTHERS?
WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO HAVE FAITH IN SOMETHING OR SOMEONE?
WHY IS HAVING FAITH IN JESUS TO DO WHAT HE PROMISED SOMETIMES HARD?

content.en: Trusting others to do things for us is hard, especially when it matters greatly. Sometimes, trusting God will be faithful to us is hard, too, especially when our lives feel uncertain or when we’re walking in tough seasons. Today, we’ll look at two people who came to Jesus with desperate faith that He could and would help them.

cultural_connection.en: Have you ever prayed for something and been disappointed that God didn’t answer the way you hoped He would? Jesus has all power and authority to heal every sickness, but as you probably know, He doesn’t always heal people physically. You may wonder why the Lord didn’t heal someone you begged for Him to heal, someone you loved deeply. You’ve seen Him heal others, so you may feel hurt—like He didn’t hear your prayers or He simply didn’t care. God loves us more than we could ever imagine, and He is going to do what is best for His glory and our good (Rom. 8:28). In fact, Jesus willingly experienced suffering and death to free us from both forever. In the moment, Jesus’s death couldn’t have looked like glory; it couldn’t have looked like what was best for His followers. But what God does is always best for His kingdom and for His people. We’ll experience disappointment, grief, and pain, but we can trust the Lord is faithful even then. Because of Jesus, believers have hope that is greater than the disappointment, grief, and pain we experience now. God hears you; He sees you; He cares for you.

title.en: We Can Take Our Desperation to Jesus

question.en: What does it mean to be desperate? Where do you turn when you feel desperate for help?

answer.en: Desperation is a feeling of hopelessness that can drive us to drastic actions. Both Jairus and the woman were desperate: Jairus wanted to save his daughter, and the woman suffered from a long, seemingly incurable disease. They had heard about Jesus’s miracles and went to Him for help. When we’re desperate, we often run to what’s powerless for help. We turn to sports or social media; we turn to harmful substances or to worldly comforts. They may make us feel better or numb our pain, but they’re powerless to save us. Instead, we can run to the Lord. He alone is powerful and faithful to save.

question.en: Why did Jesus stop to ask who touched His robe?

answer.en: Leaders: Share Context. When the Son of God asked this question, He wasn’t confused or needing clarification. Jesus asked who touched Him because He wanted to talk with the woman who had been healed. He wanted to teach an important truth to those watching and listening. Jesus didn’t shame or reprimand her for touching Him (as the law would’ve encouraged); He commended her faith! He called her “daughter”—this woman who suffered in isolation for so long. Jesus healed her physically, but more importantly, her faith in Jesus led to her spiritual healing and freed her to “go in peace.”

question.en: What does Jesus stopping for both a shunned woman and a Jewish leader help us understand about Him?

answer.en: Jesus was en route to see Jairus’s daughter when a woman interrupted His plans. Jesus stopped for her. According to the law, situations like blood exposure and touching a corpse made people “anclean” and unable to take part in community. In this text, we see Jesus stop for both a religious leader, a man of importance, and an “unclean” woman. Most people avoided interaction with the “anclean”—like this woman—because they feared being made unclean themselves. But Jesus cared more about loving people and drawing them to Himself for salvation than cultural or religious rules. Jesus was able to heal the woman and make her clean, unlike any doctor she had seen. Twelve years of pain ended because Jesus stopped for her. The Lord desires to save all people— no matter our cultural status or backgrounds, no matter how unclean our sin has made us. He doesn’t push us away. He stops for us. He draws us in. And when we come in faith, He heals us and saves us from our greatest sickness: our sin.

question.en: Jesus said the woman was saved by her faith. What does it mean to have this type of faith?

answer.en: Having faith in Jesus is more than just believing He existed as a person. When Jesus pointed to the woman’s faith, He meant that she believed Jesus was who He claimed to be and able to do what He promised. Today, we may not get to witness Jesus healing people, but Scripture shows us who Jesus is, what He has done, and what He will do. Having faith is believing that Jesus is the Son of God, that He came to live, to die on the cross, and to be raised from the dead so that we can be saved from our sin and spend eternity with Him. Placing faith in Jesus is confessing Him as Lord, as the only One who can save (Rom. 10:9-13), and results in a relationship with Him that continues to transform you from the inside out.

question.en: What do you think helped Jairus have faith, even after the news of his daughter’s death? How do you continue to have faith in difficult times?

answer.en: Jairus had faith despite hearing reports that screamed, “Give up!” If you haven’t yet, you’ll likely experience a time when faith feels pointless because of your circumstances. Notice what Jesus did just before Jairus received the news: He healed the bleeding woman. If He could do this, could He not also raise Jairus’s daughter? Wasn’t He capable? We need these examples in Scripture. Why? Because we will come to a similar crossroads: Will we believe when our circumstances shout fear and doubt? Will we recall God’s faithfulness in the past to sustain us in the present? And even when healing doesn’t come here and now, will we remember that our salvation from sin is enough?

question.en: Do you ever struggle to be open with God about your problems or fears? Why or why not?

answer.en: The woman tried to go unnoticed and trembled when Jesus asked who touched Him. Sometimes, we’re afraid to bring certain struggles to the Lord. We let our shame silence truth: God doesn’t push us away but draws near to us when we go to Him (James 4:8). This passage shows us how Jesus responds when we bring Him our honest struggles: love and grace. When you feel discouraged or ashamed, remember God’s incredible kindness toward you. He won’t turn you away. He isn’t against you; He is for you and for your freedom from sin and shame. The Lord welcomes you when you turn to Him in faith.

question.en: How can you practice relying on Jesus in both big and small moments? How could this help someone else’s faith to grow?

answer.en: Like in other relationships, learning to trust Jesus doesn’t happen by accident but must be practiced and cultivated. Trusting Him more comes through knowing Him more deeply—through His Word, through prayer, through experiencing His presence. More often than not, we remember to talk to Jesus about the huge moments in life, but we forget to talk to Him about the small moments. If we develop a habit of talking to the Lord about everything, we will more quickly turn to Him in times of desperation. And when we trust Jesus, others notice our faith and are encouraged to trust the Lord with their own struggles, pain, and shame. You don’t have to bow your head and close your eyes to stay in communication with the Lord. You can speak to Him all day! Talking with Him about small decisions will help you to trust Him more.

content.en: We live in a “prove it” kind of world. People don’t often believe without evidence, unless you can show it or demonstrate it. You claim you can do a backflip, but your friends need you to prove it. The problem with this mindset is that it stands in contrast to how things work in God’s kingdom. The Bible tells us that faith is evidence of something that is not yet seen (v. 1). Think about that for a moment. Our faith is the evidence of a reality that cannot be seen right now, a reality that is very real and alive within us. As Christians, we live with hope, or a confident expectation, of an eternal reward, as well as God’s present help right here and right now. Neither of these can be seen with our physical eyes, yet our faith is the evidence of their reality. All the heroes we read about in the Bible had this kind of faith. It was by this faith that God approved of them and by this faith that they made an impact on the world (v. 2). These men and women had a confident expectation of something to come and something unseen, but something real and alive within them. This is how God wants us to live right here and now. Like the heroes of faith, God calls us to live not based on what we can see but based on what we know is real and alive within us—our faith and our hope in Jesus.

question.en: What are examples of things you believe in but can’t see? How is this like your faith in Jesus?
Why do we lean toward the need to see before believing? How can God help you overcome this?

prayer.en: God, I decide today to live based on what I know to be true, not on what I can see with my eyes. Help me rest in You and what I know to be true.

content.en: Have you ever really wanted to make someone happy? Maybe you wanted a friend or family member to have the best day possible on their birthday. Or maybe you wanted someone to be proud of you. Think about a coach, teacher, or parent that you wanted to see your effort and think you were doing a good job. Did you know that this should be our heart toward God? As Christians, our highest aim should be to honor God, to please Him, and to live in a way that brings Him joy. The Bible tells us exactly how we do this! Through faith. Not through striving or checking boxes or putting on a good face. Faith! Without faith, we can’t please God. Faith isn’t optional but essential in pleasing the Lord. Why? Because faith believes that God exists, that He is who He says He is, and that His promises are true. Faith trusts that God really does reward those who seek after Him. When we believe God and respond by seeking Him in obedience, our lives honor Him. When the way we live reflects that we believe God is real and we choose to follow Him, God is pleased, overjoyed, proud. And He promises to reward this kind of faith-filled life! So, in the same way that we desire to bring our friends and loved ones joy, we should live with that same intentionality toward God. Live by faith. Trust Him. Seek Him. Walk with confidence that He is who He says He is and that He will do everything He has promised to do.

question.en: Based on Hebrews 11:6, how would you describe what faith is and how to walk in it?
What are practical ways that you can demonstrate faith in God and live a life that pleases Him?

prayer.en: God, I want to make You proud. I want my life to give You joy. Help me to live a life that is rooted in faith and in Your promise to reward those who seek after You.

content.en: Have you ever failed at something you tried really hard to do? You gave it your best effort, yet you still couldn’t accomplish it. No matter how talented or dedicated we are, we all fail at times. We have all fallen short of what we hoped to accomplish. This goes for sin too. No matter how much we've tried to live according to God’s commands, we have all sinned and fallen short of the glory of God (Rom. 3:23). So, what is sin? Sin is simply missing the mark God has for us, like aiming at a target and failing to hit it. God has set a perfect standard, and even in our best efforts and on our best days, we miss the mark. No matter how hard we try, we can’t reach God’s standard because He is perfectly holy. This is why we need a Savior, someone to lift the burden of God’s law off our shoulders by living it perfectly, someone to free us from the consequences of our sin by paying our penalty. God’s perfect law reveals what is required for eternal life and a right relationship with God. The law is good; it points us to God and reveals His nature to us (v. 24). But because of our inability to keep God’s law perfectly, it also exposes our sinful nature and shows us that we are imprisoned by our sin and its consequences (v. 23)—that is, until Jesus came and did for us what we could never do for ourselves. He lived the life we cannot live. He became the perfect sacrifice for sin, died the death we deserved, and through His resurrection, freed us from the power of sin. Now, through faith in Christ, we are sons and daughters of God and are declared righteous before Him! What an exchange! As sons and daughters who have been fully and freely forgiven, we can now live in intimate relationship with God, both today and forevermore.

question.en: What does the Bible show us about God’s nature, His standard for us, and how we fall short?
Why is Jesus’s life, death, and resurrection good news?

prayer.en: JESUS, THANK YOU FOR YOUR FINISHED WORK ON THE CROSS. THANK YOU FOR LOVING ME, FOR TAKING MY PLACE, AND FOR BRINGING ME INTO A RIGHT RELATIONSHIP WITH GOD.

content.en: Comparison may be more damaging to us socially than anything else. Many people live their whole lives comparing themselves to others: how they look, how they dress, their achievements, their abilities, and even their morality. We compare ourselves to others to see how we measure up and how others measure up to us. Comparison is such a normal part of our culture that even followers of Jesus are often trapped in it. But Jesus doesn’t want us to live this way. Why? Comparison can cause us to show favoritism to one person and mistreat another person. When we live in comparison and people don’t measure up to the standard we have decided they must meet, we treat them differently than those who do meet our standard. One way we can guard our lives from comparison and favoritism is by remembering that we are all sinners in the same position of need before God. God chose the least and the lowly to be heirs of His kingdom (v. 5). When we remember our common ground at the foot of the cross, that we are all in need of a Savior and saved by grace and grace alone, comparison and favoritism have no room in our hearts. Instead of looking at everyone else to see how we compare, we should live with our eyes fixed on Jesus, recognizing our constant need for Him. When we stop measuring ourselves and others by human standards and instead measure everything by the grace of God, comparison loses its power. Grace levels the ground, frees our hearts, and teaches us to love people, not for how they measure up but for who they are— people created in God’s image and deeply loved by Him.

question.en: In what ways do you compare yourself to others? How are you tempted to show favoritism?
What are ways you can guard your heart against comparison and favoritism?

prayer.en: God, I repent for the times I have shown favoritism to someone over another. Help me remember that we are saved by grace and not by our own good works.

content.en: Imagine this: You are sitting in a restaurant enjoying your food when suddenly someone starts shouting. As you look up and begin to listen, you hear these words: “Anyone who comes to the front and gets in line gets a million dollars!” Now let’s imagine that you really needed some money. In fact, you were thinking about it before all the commotion. If you believed that person, you would get up, get in line, and excitedly wait for your fortune. Okay, so that probably will never happen. However, it is a great illustration of how faith and works go hand in hand. We are not saved by our good works because our efforts and abilities will always fall short. We are saved by placing our faith in Jesus and in His finished work on the cross (Eph. 2:8-9). However, our faith should be evident in our actions. In the imagined scenario of getting a million dollars just for standing in line, your faith in the person’s promise is proven by your action of getting in line. In the same way, our faith in Jesus is exhibited by our obedience to Him. When we say that we believe Jesus is Lord, what proves our faith is following Him as Lord. When we claim Jesus is the Lord of our lives yet continue to live as if we are the rulers of our lives, then we exhibit what the Bible calls “dead” faith (v. 17). In other words, our claim is empty; our faith isn’t revealed in our lives. Not only are we called to live out our faith, we have every good reason to do so. God is good; His Son died for our sin. Why would we live any other way? Why would we settle for lives that only pledge faith in our words and not our actions? Let’s demonstrate our faith through daily obedience to Jesus. When we do, people won't need explanations or arguments. Our lives will be the evidence—faith in action (v. 18).

question.en: How do actions reflect belief?
What areas of your life don’t align with what you say you believe?

prayer.en: God, help me to see any areas of my life where what I say I believe doesn’t line up with how I live. Help my faith in You grow, and as it does, let my life reveal it.
